text_blocks.snippet: Type 2 diabetes often develops slowly over years, and many people have no symptoms in the early stages. When early signs do appear, they are often subtle and can be easy to dismiss.
snippet_highlighted_words: they are often subtle and can be easy to dismiss

list.snippet: Frequent urination (polyuria): You visit the bathroom more often than usual, especially at night, as your kidneys try to flush out extra glucose from your blood.
Excessive thirst (polydipsia): Because you lose more fluid through frequent urination, you feel constantly thirsty.
Persistent fatigue: Your cells cannot properly absorb glucose to use for fuel, leaving you feeling tired and worn out even after resting.
Blurred vision: High blood sugar can cause temporary fluid shifts and swelling in the lenses of your eyes.
Slow-healing sores or cuts: Elevated blood sugar impairs circulation and weakens your immune response, making minor injuries take much longer to heal.
Tingling or numbness: Mild nerve irritation or damage (peripheral neuropathy) can cause a pins-and-needles sensation, tingling, or numbness in your hands or feet.

Unexplained weight changes: Your body may burn fat and muscle for energy instead of glucose, leading to unexpected weight loss, or you might experience insulin-related weight gain (especially around the abdomen).
Frequent infections: Bacteria and fungi thrive on extra sugar, leading to recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs), yeast infections, or skin issues.
Darkened skin patches (acanthosis nigricans): Velvety, dark patches of skin can form in body folds like the neck, armpits, or groin as a sign of heavy insulin resistance.

text_blocks.snippet: Because type 2 diabetes is so quiet early on, routine screening is important if you are over 45 or have risk factors like a family history, high blood pressure, or a sedentary lifestyle.
A doctor can diagnose it using simple blood tests through the Cleveland Clinic Health Guide or your primary care provider:

list.snippet: Fasting plasma glucose test (126 mg/dL or higher)
A1C test measuring average blood sugar over 2 to 3 months (6.5% or higher)
Random plasma glucose test (200 mg/dL or higher)
